solution:
(a) At every point of a charge-free region the electric field has one definite magnitude and one definite direction: a test charge placed there experiences a single force, so \(\vec{E}\) is a well-defined vector at that point. A field line is nothing but the curve traced out by stepping along that direction from point to neighbouring point, so as long as the field exists the curve can always be continued — there is no point at which it can simply stop. A sudden break would mean the direction of \(\vec{E}\) jumped discontinuously with nothing there to cause it: a charge moving along the line would have to change the direction of its acceleration abruptly in empty space. Field lines can begin or end only where charge sits — they start on positive charge and terminate on negative charge (or run off to infinity) — so in the space between the charges no line can break off.

(b) Suppose two field lines crossed at a point P. Two different tangents could then be drawn at P, so the electric field at P would have two directions at the same time. That is impossible: a test charge placed at P experiences a force in one definite direction only, and \(\vec{E}\) at a point is a single vector. Hence two field lines can never intersect. (The one place where the direction is genuinely undefined is a null point, where \(E = 0\) — and no field line passes through such a point, so it is not a counter-example.)

(a) Because \(\vec{E}\) is uniquely defined and continuous at every point of a charge-free region, a field line can always be continued and can terminate only on a charge; a break would make the field direction discontinuous where there is no charge.
(b) Because two crossing lines would give two tangents, hence two directions of \(\vec{E}\), at the same point — but the field at a point has only one direction.

Convert to SI: separation \(AB = 20\,\text{cm} = 0.20\,\text{m}\), so the midpoint O is at \(r = 0.10\,\text{m}\) from each charge; \(q_{A} = 3\,\mu\text{C} = 3 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{C}\) and \(q_{B} = -3\,\mu\text{C} = -3 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{C}\).

(a) For a point charge, \(E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\dfrac{|q|}{r^{2}}\).

Field at O due to A: \(E_{A} = \dfrac{(9 \times 10^{9})(3 \times 10^{-6})}{(0.10)^{2}} = 2.7 \times 10^{6}\,\text{N C}^{-1}\), directed away from the positive charge A, that is from A towards B.

Field at O due to B: \(E_{B} = \dfrac{(9 \times 10^{9})(3 \times 10^{-6})}{(0.10)^{2}} = 2.7 \times 10^{6}\,\text{N C}^{-1}\), directed towards the negative charge B, that is also from A towards B.

The two fields point the same way, so they add:
\(E = 2.7 \times 10^{6} + 2.7 \times 10^{6} = 5.4 \times 10^{6}\,\text{N C}^{-1}\), along AB from A to B.

(b) The magnitude of the force on the test charge is \(F = |q|E = (1.5 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{C})(5.4 \times 10^{6}\,\text{N C}^{-1}) = 8.1 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{N}\). Since the test charge is negative, the force is antiparallel to \(\vec{E}\), so it acts from B towards A.

(a) \(E = 5.4 \times 10^{6}\,\text{N C}^{-1}\), directed along AB from the positive charge A towards the negative charge B.
(b) \(F = 8.1 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{N}\), directed along BA — from B towards A, opposite to the field, because the test charge is negative.

Total charge is the algebraic sum of the two charges:
\(q = q_{A} + q_{B} = 2.5 \times 10^{-7} + \left(-2.5 \times 10^{-7}\right) = 0\).

The two equal and opposite charges lie on the z-axis, separated by
\(2a = 15\,\text{cm} + 15\,\text{cm} = 30\,\text{cm} = 0.30\,\text{m}\).

For a pair of charges \(\pm q\) a distance \(2a\) apart, \(p = q\,(2a)\) with q the magnitude of either charge:
\(p = \left(2.5 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{C}\right)\left(0.30\,\text{m}\right) = 7.5 \times 10^{-8}\,\text{C m}\).

By convention \(\vec{p}\) points from the negative charge to the positive charge. Here the negative charge B is at \(z = +15\,\text{cm}\) and the positive charge A at \(z = -15\,\text{cm}\), so \(\vec{p}\) is directed from B to A, i.e. along the negative z-direction:
\(\vec{p} = -7.5 \times 10^{-8}\,\hat{k}\,\text{C m}\).

Total charge \(= 0\).
Electric dipole moment \(p = 7.5 \times 10^{-8}\,\text{C m}\), directed along the negative z-axis (from B towards A, i.e. from the negative charge to the positive charge).

A dipole in a uniform field experiences a torque \(\vec{\tau} = \vec{p} \times \vec{E}\), whose magnitude is
\(\tau = pE\sin\theta\),
where \(\theta\) is the angle between \(\vec{p}\) and \(\vec{E}\).

Here \(p = 4 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{C m}\), \(E = 5 \times 10^{4}\,\text{N C}^{-1}\) and \(\theta = 30^{\circ}\), so

\(\tau = \left(4 \times 10^{-9}\right)\left(5 \times 10^{4}\right)\sin 30^{\circ} = \left(2 \times 10^{-4}\right)(0.5)\,\text{N m}\).

\(\tau = 1 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{N m}\)

In the figure the upper plate is positively charged and the lower plate negatively charged, so between the plates the electric field runs from the positive plate to the negative plate — vertically downward.

A positive charge is pushed along \(\vec{E}\), i.e. downward, towards the negatively charged plate; a negative charge is pushed opposite to \(\vec{E}\), i.e. upward, towards the positively charged plate.

Tracks 1 and 2 both bend upward, towards the positive plate, so particles 1 and 2 must carry negative charge. Track 3 bends downward, towards the negative plate, so particle 3 carries positive charge.

For the deflection: inside the plates a particle of charge q and mass m has a constant transverse acceleration \(a = qE/m\), while its horizontal velocity v is unchanged, so it spends a time \(t = L/v\) crossing a field region of length L. The sideways displacement on emerging is
\(y = \dfrac{1}{2}at^{2} = \dfrac{qEL^{2}}{2mv^{2}}\).

For particles that enter with the same speed and traverse the same length of the same field, \(y \propto q/m\) — the more a track is deflected, the larger its charge-to-mass ratio. Track 3 shows the greatest deflection of the three, so particle 3 has the highest charge-to-mass ratio.

Particles 1 and 2 carry negative charge; particle 3 carries positive charge. Particle 3 has the highest charge-to-mass ratio.
_note: Ex 1.13 reads its data off Fig. 1.30 (upper plate marked +, lower plate marked -; tracks 1 and 2 curve up towards the + plate, track 2 less than track 1; track 3 curves down towards the - plate with the largest deflection). The deflection comparison assumes the three particles enter with the same speed and cross the same length of field, which is what the figure shows; NCERT does not state it explicitly, and the solution says so.
